reviews.reason: Both explain narrow-width spatial filtering and conditional sequential evaluation. A's 'successive combined designs' and B's 'conditional on earlier modifications' reflect P09 Secs. 2.1, 2.4-2.6 and Fig. 4: fixed training, pre-expansion depthwise filtering, and normalized downsampling. B foregrounds affordability slightly more directly, but neither has a substantive explanatory advantage.

B's 'same primitives to support optimization and fast rasterization' makes the representation-renderer coupling clearer than A's 'accessible to a differentiable tile rasterizer' (P10 Secs. 4-6). Both faithfully report Table 1's A6000 throughput and mixed Mip-NeRF360 metrics, with storage and artifacts supported by Sec. 7.4. B organizes these into a stronger abstract-level contribution.

A's 'without a fixed primitive-count cutoff' and B's opacity reconstruction accurately summarize P10 Sec. 6. Both connect real-time rendering to metric-dependent quality and storage costs (Table 1; Sec. 7.4). A names the datasets and appearance encoding; B states the LPIPS comparison. These supported selection differences do not establish a meaningful abstract-level winner.

A's 'dense channel transformations carry most of the work' matches P09 Sec. 2.5's rationale for moving depthwise filtering before expansion. B explains the same ordering through its reduced channel count. Both accurately connect simplified blocks and normalized downsampling to the fixed-recipe sequential evaluation (Secs. 2.1, 2.6; Fig. 4). Their methodological explanations are effectively equivalent.

A's 'avoiding variable-length per-pixel histories' and B's 'extra per-pixel storage constant' express the same backward-pass advantage documented in P10 Sec. 6. Both accurately connect tile sorting, approximate visibility, reverse traversal, image loss, and gradient-guided densification (Secs. 5.1-5.2). B spells out duplication and thresholds; A emphasizes acquiring detail. Neither materially improves the methods explanation.

A explains size-dependent cloning and splitting; B emphasizes that the 'same differentiable rasterizer supports reconstruction and subsequent viewing.' Both are grounded in P10 Secs. 4-6 and summarize the contribution clearly. Table 1 supports their quality and throughput comparisons, and Sec. 7.4 supports storage and coverage limitations. These complementary emphases leave the abstracts closely matched.

A's 'convolutional route to competitive recognition' and B's 'convolutional alternative for the evaluated recognition tasks' draw similarly bounded conclusions. P09 Secs. 2.1 and 2.5 support their fixed-training and narrow-width kernel explanations; Table 1 verifies both classification examples, and Sec. 4 supports downstream competitiveness. B makes the initial training step slightly more explicit, without changing the abstract's explanatory strength.

B's 'interactive display at competitive quality' connects Table 1's metric-dependent comparison to the practical contribution and storage cost. Its Truck cutoff result directly tests whether an optimization shortcut preserves quality (P10 Sec. 7.3; Table 3). A is accurate, but its intervening Tanks & Temples budget comparison makes the results argument less unified.

Both connect classification accuracy and measured throughput (P09 Table 1) to COCO transfer (Table 3), then interpret neutral or unstable roadmap changes (Secs. 2.5-2.6). A's 'evaluated combination' emphasizes conditional attribution; B's 'condition of the reported downsampling result' specifies stabilization. Both synthesize the evidence rather than merely listing gains, with no meaningful difference in results-paragraph quality.

B's 'accelerating display through a fixed gradient cutoff' blurs training and inference: P10 Sec. 7.3 tests skipping gradients to speed optimization, not display. This warrants a localized fidelity concern, not rejection of the method description. A relates reverse traversal directly to gradient support and memory, matching Sec. 6; both otherwise match Secs. 5-6.

Both explain the strengthened baseline and convolutional redesign before presenting classification, scaling, and transfer evidence (P09 Sec. 2.1; Table 1; Sec. 4). A's multimodal and structured-output boundary is supported by Limitations F. B's conclusion is already bounded to 'these recognition tasks.' The extra caveat does not make A inherently better; both convey the central contribution clearly.

A's 'prediction quality rather than the classification speed benefit' distinguishes what the downstream comparisons establish (P09 Tables 1, 3, 4). Both correctly qualify EfficientNetV2-L's different 480 x 480 setting. B's closing return to its higher classification score adds less to interpreting the COCO/ADE20K results. All reported values and evaluation conditions are supported.

A's 'storage per pixel need not grow' and B's 'without a predetermined count limit' capture complementary requirements established in P10 Sec. 6. Both explain tile duplication, shared sorting, opacity saturation, reverse traversal, and approximate blending with accurate causal links. A foregrounds gradient preservation; B foregrounds shared visibility work. These are equally effective explanations of the rasterizer.

Both interpret the same quality-throughput-storage tradeoff accurately (P10 Table 1), and both identify Truck's gradient-cap failure (Sec. 7.3; Table 3). B's 'separate Truck ablation using manually downsampled inputs' supplies useful provenance from the table caption; A already distinguishes Truck from the preceding dataset averages. A's popping explanation matches Sec. 7.4. Their results arguments remain near-equivalent.

A's 'competitive alternative to Swin in these workloads' and B's 'Transformer-style organization without relying on self-attention' both reflect P09's closing remarks in Sec. 2.6. Their narrow-width kernel rationale and classification/scaling examples match Sec. 2.5 and Table 1; Sec. 4 supports transfer. A emphasizes conditional attribution, B the organizing question. Neither offers a decisive abstract-level advantage.

A's 'coordinated redesign' and B's 'tested activation layout' are both supported by P09 Sec. 2.6: GELU substitution is neutral, fewer activations help, and normalized separate downsampling reaches 82.0%. Both distinguish this roadmap result from Table 3's pretrained COCO comparison and preserve conditional attribution. A leads with synthesis; B builds from the strengthened baseline. Both fulfill the results function.

Both accurately place LayerNorm before the pointwise layers and GELU between them (P09 Fig. 4; Sec. 2.6), explaining why depthwise filtering precedes fourfold expansion (Secs. 2.4-2.5). A's 'configuration already reached' and B's 'conditional on the preceding architecture' equally characterize the fixed-recipe roadmap. Their block, hierarchy, and evaluation descriptions are precise and comparably readable.

Both turn Table 1's training-budget comparison and Table 3's gradient-cap ablation into coherent tradeoff arguments. A's 'matched-GPU speedup' caution is supported by P10 Sec. 7.2, footnote 2; B's 'manually downsampled inputs' matches Table 3's caption. Neither makes an unsupported timing comparison, and both retain Sec. 7.4's limitations. These different contextual choices do not break the near tie.
